p: Two of the oldest copies say the centurion is "placed" under authority, the word Luke uses (Luke 7:8).

readings.w: Ephraemi (C, 400s), most Greek manuscripts and the Byzantine text (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Textus Receptus
Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s), a few others, most Old Latin manuscripts, Chrysostom and Hilary (Tischendorf); Westcott-Hort

why: "Placed" is exactly Luke's word, and copyists often made Matthew and Luke agree. Most editors think it came in from Luke 7:8, even though two very old copies have it.
b: The meaning is the same either way: the centurion both obeys orders and gives them.

a: I have not met faith this great in anyone in Israel
t: "In no one in Israel" or "not even in Israel"?
p: The KJV's "not even in Israel" is the wording of Luke 7:9. Vaticanus and several early translations have "with no one in Israel."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), a few minuscules, some Old Latin manuscripts, the Coptic versions, the Curetonian Syriac, Ambrose and Augustine (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: παρ’ οὐδενὶ τοσαύτην πίστιν ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ εὗρον
readings.en: with no one in Israel have I found such faith
readings.plain: I have not met faith this great in anyone in Israel

readings.w: Ephraemi (C, 400s), most later Greek manuscripts, the Vulgate and most Old Latin, Origen (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel")
readings.orig: οὐδὲ ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ τοσαύτην πίστιν εὗρον
readings.en: not even in Israel have I found such faith
readings.plain: I have not met faith this great, not even in Israel

why: "Not even in Israel" is exactly Luke's wording (Luke 7:9), and copyists often made parallel Gospels agree. A change away from the familiar Lukan form is hard to explain, so most editors keep "with no one."
b: The meaning hardly changes, but the KJV form sounds sharper against Israel.

a: The servant was healed in that same hour.
p: Some manuscripts add a sentence from Luke 7:10 at the end of the verse.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s), most Greek manuscripts and the Byzantine text (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: καὶ ἰάθη ὁ παῖς ἐν τῇ ὥρᾳ ἐκείνῃ.
readings.en: and the servant was healed in that hour
readings.plain: The servant was healed in that same hour.

readings.w: Ephraemi (C, 400s), the later uncials M, U and X, more than fifty minuscules, and the Harclean Syriac and Ethiopic versions (Tischendorf)
readings.orig: καὶ ἰάθη ὁ παῖς ἐν τῇ ὥρᾳ ἐκείνῃ. καὶ ὑποστρέψας ὁ ἑκατόνταρχος εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ εὗρεν τὸν παῖδα ὑγιαίνοντα.
readings.en: and the servant was healed in that hour. And the centurion, having returned to his house in that same hour, found the servant well.
readings.plain: The servant was healed in that same hour. When the centurion went back to his house in that same hour, he found the servant well.

why: The extra sentence echoes Luke 7:10, where the messengers return and find the slave well. It is an early attempt to round off Matthew's story, but most witnesses lack it.
b: Tischendorf notes that some copies mark the sentence with asterisks, a scribe's sign for doubtful words.

p: Matthew has her serve "him"; the KJV, following some copies, says "them," as in Mark.

readings.w: Vaticanus (B, 300s), Ephraemi (C, 400s), most later Greek manuscripts, Origen (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
The uncials L and Δ and the first hand of M, the Old Latin, the Vulgate and the Curetonian Syriac (Tischendorf); Textus Receptus (KJV "ministered unto them")

why: "Him" has the stronger Greek support. "Them" is an easy change to match Mark 1:31 and Luke 4:39, and the Latin translations spread it in the West.

p: The SBL and Tyndale House editions read "large crowds"; Westcott-Hort and NA28 read simply "a crowd."

readings.w: Ephraemi (C, 400s), L and most later Greek manuscripts (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, SBLGNT, THGNT, Textus Receptus
Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s) (Tischendorf); Westcott-Hort, NA28
Three minuscules, some Old Latin manuscripts and the Sahidic Coptic (Tischendorf)

why: The short reading rests mainly on Vaticanus, and NA28 prefers it as the one that best explains the others. The SBL and Tyndale House editors judged the wide support for "large crowds" stronger, and the Plain English Translation follows them. The sense of the verse does not change.
b: A few copies leave out either "crowds" or "many," more signs that copyists adjusted the phrase in several ways.

p: The KJV says "his disciples came to him... Lord, save us." Vaticanus lacks "his disciples," and Vaticanus and Ephraemi lack "us."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), several Old Latin manuscripts, some Vulgate manuscripts, and the Sahidic and Bohairic Coptic (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: προσελθόντες ἤγειραν αὐτὸν λέγοντες· Κύριε, σῶσον
readings.en: having come, they woke him, saying, Lord, save

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus as first written (300s, which seems to have had "his disciples"), a corrector of Ephraemi, most later manuscripts (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "his disciples came to him... Lord, save us")
readings.orig: προσελθόντες οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ ἤγειραν αὐτὸν λέγοντες· Κύριε, σῶσον ἡμᾶς
readings.en: his disciples, having come, woke him, saying, Lord, save us

why: Copyists tended to make the subject explicit and to complete the cry with "us." The Plain English Translation supplies "us" anyway, since English needs it, so only "his disciples" changes the wording.
b: The two additions do not travel together. "Us" is missing in Vaticanus, Ephraemi and the minuscules 1, 13, 118 and 209, but found in most later uncials (Tischendorf).

p: The three Gospels and their manuscripts disagree on the region. The KJV has "Gergesenes" here.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), Ephraemi as first written (400s), M, Δ, about ten more, the Syriac versions, Eusebius and Epiphanius (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
A corrector of Ephraemi, most later uncials (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
The Old Latin and the Vulgate, the Sahidic Coptic, Athanasius and Hilary; most copies known to Origen (Tischendorf). It is also the reading of Mark 5:1 and Luke 8:26 in their oldest copies

why: In Matthew the best evidence reads "Gadarenes," while Mark and Luke read "Gerasenes" in their oldest copies. Each Gospel was probably copied toward the others. "Gergesenes" spread after Origen (about AD 240) argued that neither Gadara nor Gerasa lay on the lake, and proposed a place called Gergesa on the shore.
b: Gadara, a city of the Decapolis, lay about six miles southeast of the lake, and Josephus says its territory reached the shore. Gerasa (modern Jerash) is over thirty miles away. A site on the east shore at Kursi, with a large Byzantine monastery, has long been linked with Gergesa. Codex Sinaiticus as first written reads "Gazarenes," a further slip (Tischendorf). The geography fits Matthew's "Gadarenes" well: the herd needed only a steep slope near the water within the city's land.

p: The KJV reads "Jesus, thou Son of God." Vaticanus and other early witnesses do not have the name.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), L, about twenty more, several Old Latin manuscripts, the Coptic, Origen and Cyprian (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
A corrector of Ephraemi, most later uncials (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The name was probably added from Mark 5:7 and Luke 8:28, where the demons say "Jesus." Adding a familiar name is a common copying habit.

p: The KJV's "suffer us to go away" follows the later text. Vaticanus and the early translations have "send us."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), the minuscules 1, 22, 33 and 118, the Coptic, most Old Latin and the Vulgate (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
Ephraemi (C, 400s), most later uncials, the Syriac and Gothic (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "suffer us to go away into")
readings.plain: allow us to go off into

why: "Allow us to go" matches the wording of Luke 8:32, and Gospel parallels were often brought into line. The demons' bolder "send us" is the harder reading.

p: The editions split: SBL and Tyndale House read "knowing" their thoughts, NA28 and the Byzantine text "seeing."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), M, about sixty minuscules, both main Syriac versions, the Sahidic Coptic, the Gothic and Chrysostom (Tischendorf); SBLGNT, THGNT, Westcott-Hort
Ephraemi (C, 400s), Bezae (D, about 400), most later uncials, the Bohairic Coptic, the Old Latin and the Vulgate (Tischendorf); NA28, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus

why: The two Greek words differ by one letter, and both are old. "Knowing their thoughts" is the more natural phrase (12:25 has it), which may favor "seeing" as the harder reading, but the Plain English Translation follows the SBL and Tyndale House editors. English readers lose little either way: Jesus perceives what they are thinking.
b: With "saw," the Plain English Translation would read "Jesus saw their thoughts." The Byzantine text also adds "you" (ὑμεῖς) before "thinking," so the KJV reads "Wherefore think ye evil." Vaticanus, Ephraemi and Bezae lack it (Tischendorf).

p: The older copies say the crowds were afraid. Later ones, and the KJV, say they "marveled."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), Bezae (D, about 400), the minuscules 1, 22, 33, 59 and 118, the Old Latin, the Vulgate, the Coptic and Syriac versions, Hilary (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
Ephraemi (C, 400s), most later uncials, the Harclean Syriac (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "they marvelled")

why: Fear seemed an odd reaction to a healing, so copyists softened it to wonder. The reverse change is hard to explain, and "afraid" has the older and wider support.

p: The KJV adds "to repentance," from Luke 5:32. The older manuscripts of Matthew do not have it.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), Bezae (D, about 400), V, Δ, the minuscules 1, 22, 33, 118 and 209, the Syriac, most Old Latin, the Vulgate, Basil and Jerome (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
Ephraemi (C, 400s), most later uncials, the Coptic, a few Old Latin manuscripts, Hilary (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "but sinners to repentance")
readings.plain: I came to call sinners to repentance.

why: Luke 5:32 has "to repentance," and the phrase was added here to match. Matthew's shorter saying fits his meal setting: Jesus "calls" sinners as a host invites guests.

p: A few manuscripts, Vaticanus among them, lack "a great deal." NA28 prints the word in brackets.

readings.w: Ephraemi (C, 400s), Bezae (D, about 400), most later manuscripts and all the early translations (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, SBLGNT, THGNT; NA28 in brackets
Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s) and three others (Tischendorf); Metzger adds the first hand of Sinaiticus

why: The word has wide support, and a copyist could have dropped it by accident or to match Mark 2:18. Its absence from Vaticanus leaves real doubt, which is why NA28 brackets it.
b: According to Metzger, a corrector of Sinaiticus wrote pykna, "often," from Luke 5:33.

p: Codex Bezae and many early translations have the groom's friends unable to "fast" rather than "grieve."

readings.w: Vaticanus, Ephraemi and nearly all Greek manuscripts (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Textus Receptus
Bezae (D, about 400), the minuscule 61, many early versions, Chrysostom and Hilary (Tischendorf)

why: "Fast" is the word in Mark 2:19 and Luke 5:34, and it fits the question about fasting, so copyists changed Matthew's "grieve" to match. Matthew's word ties fasting to mourning: a fast is a sign of grief, out of place at a wedding.
b: Bezae also adds "in those days" at the end of the verse, from Luke 5:35 (Tischendorf).

a: But the Pharisees kept saying, "He throws out the demons with the help of the ruler of the demons."
t: A missing verse in a few witnesses
p: Codex Bezae, two Old Latin manuscripts and Hilary leave out this whole verse.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), Ephraemi (C, 400s) and all other Greek manuscripts but one (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus

readings.en: But the Pharisees were saying, By the ruler of the demons he casts out the demons.
readings.plain: But the Pharisees kept saying, "He throws out the demons with the help of the ruler of the demons."

readings.w: Codex Bezae (D, about 400), the Old Latin manuscripts a and k, and Hilary (Tischendorf)

why: The verse is in almost every manuscript. Some scholars think it was added from 12:24, but it prepares for 10:25, where Jesus refers to this very charge, so most editors keep it.
b: Some Old Latin manuscripts name the ruler of the demons here: "Beelzebul" (Tischendorf).

a: every kind of disease and illness.
p: The KJV adds "among the people," from 4:23. The older copies of 9:35 lack it.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), Ephraemi as first written (400s), Bezae (D, about 400), S, Δ, the minuscules 1, 22, 33, 118, 157 and 209, about fifty more, and most early versions (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.plain: every kind of disease and illness.

readings.plain: every kind of disease and illness among the people.

why: Matthew 4:23 ends "among the people," and scribes made the two summaries match. Some manuscripts add still more here.
b: L, the minuscules 13, 124 and 262 and several Old Latin manuscripts add "and many followed him" (Tischendorf).

p: The KJV says the crowds "fainted." That follows a different Greek word found in a few late copies.

readings.w: Vaticanus (B, 300s), Ephraemi (C, 400s), Bezae (D, about 400), most later uncials, about 150 minuscules, the Old Latin and the Vulgate ("harassed"), Basil and Chrysostom (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
The uncial L and some others (Tischendorf); Textus Receptus (KJV "they fainted")

why: "Harassed" has almost all the evidence, including the Byzantine text. "Worn out" may come from Mark 8:3 and Matthew 15:32, where the same word describes hungry crowds who might faint on the way.

p: The KJV has "Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus." Vaticanus and several early translations have only "Thaddaeus."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), the minuscules 17 and 124, the Coptic, several Old Latin manuscripts and the Vulgate (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
The first hand of Ephraemi (400s), most later uncials (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
Codex Bezae (D, about 400), the minuscule 122, the Old Latin manuscript k, copies known to Augustine, and Origen as reported by Rufinus (Tischendorf)

why: "Thaddaeus" agrees with Mark 3:18 and has the oldest Greek support. The fuller Byzantine reading looks like a combination of the two older forms.
b: Several Old Latin manuscripts read "Judas the Zealot" here (Tischendorf). Luke and Acts have "Judas son of James" in this place (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13). See the note on 10:3.

p: The KJV's "Simon the Canaanite" follows a different spelling of the Greek name.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), Ephraemi (C, 400s), Bezae (D, about 400), L, the minuscules 1, 22, 33 and 118, the Old Latin, the Vulgate and the Bohairic Coptic (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
Most later uncials and the Sahidic Coptic (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "Simon the Canaanite")

why: Both spellings come from the Aramaic word for "zealous." The ending -itēs usually marks a person from a place, so the later spelling led readers to think of Cana or Canaan.
b: See the note on 10:4 for what "Cananaean" means.

a: Cure those who are ill, raise the dead,
p: Most later Greek manuscripts leave out "raise the dead." The older copies have it, and so does the KJV, in a different place in the list.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), Ephraemi as first written (400s), Bezae (D, about 400), about fifteen more, most Old Latin, the Vulgate and the Bohairic Coptic (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.en: heal the sick, raise the dead
readings.plain: Cure those who are ill, raise the dead,

readings.w: A corrector of Ephraemi, most later uncials, about 150 minuscules, the Sahidic Coptic, Eusebius, Athanasius, Basil and Chrysostom (Tischendorf); Byzantine text (the Robinson-Pierpont edition)

why: The phrase has the oldest support. It may have dropped out because the nearby verbs end alike, or because copyists did not read of the Twelve raising anyone.
b: Where the phrase is found, it moves around. The Textus Receptus puts it after "cleanse the lepers" (KJV: "Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils"), and a few copies put it last (Tischendorf). So the KJV agrees with the older manuscripts on including the words, but not on their place.

p: The KJV's "nor yet staves" follows the plural. Vaticanus and Bezae have one staff.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), Bezae (D, about 400), most Old Latin manuscripts and the Vulgate (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
Ephraemi (C, 400s), most later uncials, about 150 minuscules, the Old Latin manuscripts a and k, the Peshitta Syriac (Tischendorf); Byzantine text (KJV "nor yet staves")

why: The plural may have been an attempt to reconcile Matthew with Mark 6:8, which allows one staff: take no extra staffs. The singular is the harder reading, and the editors who print it judge it original, though the plural has wide support.
b: Printed editions differ here. Tischendorf himself printed the plural, and he reports the singular for the Elzevir edition of the Textus Receptus.

p: Several old witnesses add the words of the greeting, "Peace to this house," from Luke 10:5.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), Ephraemi (C, 400s), most later uncials (Tischendorf); Byzantine text, NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Textus Receptus
Bezae (D, about 400), L, the minuscules 1, 22 and 209, more than fifty others, the Old Latin, the Vulgate and Hilary (Tischendorf)
readings.orig: ἀσπάσασθε αὐτήν λέγοντες· Εἰρήνη τῷ οἴκῳ τούτῳ
readings.en: greet it, saying, Peace to this house
readings.plain: greet the household, saying, 'Peace to this house.'

why: The words are an explanation that a scribe could easily add from Luke 10:5. Most editors think the shorter text is original, though the addition is early and widespread.

t: "And if they persecute you in the next..."
p: Some witnesses carry the saying one step further: if they persecute you in the next town, flee to another.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s), Ephraemi (C, 400s), most later uncials, the Vulgate, the Coptic, Syriac and Gothic, Clement and Origen (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus
Bezae (D, about 400), L, the minuscules 1, 13, 22, 118, 124, 209 and 247, several Old Latin manuscripts, Origen, Athanasius and Hilary (Tischendorf)
readings.orig: φεύγετε εἰς τὴν ἑτέραν· κἂν ἐν τῇ ἑτέρᾳ διώκωσιν ὑμᾶς, φεύγετε εἰς τὴν ἄλλην
readings.en: flee to the other; and if they persecute you in the other, flee to another
readings.plain: escape to the next. And if they hunt you down in the next, escape to another.

why: The longer form looks like a natural expansion, and the shorter text has much stronger support.
b: The Greek words differ slightly within each group without changing the English. The SBL and NA28 texts read heteran ("the other") with Vaticanus; the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus read allēn ("another"). In the longer form, L and some others read "if they persecute you out of this one" (ek tautēs), and Bezae has its own wording (Tischendorf).
